strengths: Synth-SBDH addresses a practical clinical NLP need: accessible training data for extracting social and behavioral determinants of health. Its 8,767 examples cover 14 SBDH categories plus pain, with spans, presence, temporality, and rationales. The resource contribution is useful even without a novel generation algorithm.

The central claim that synthetic pretraining can improve real-data classification is well supported. For example, prompt-based RoBERTa improves from 55.64 to 91.11 macro-F on MIMIC-SBDH, while standard RoBERTa improves from 72.38 to 80.71 on VA-SBDH. These are substantial downstream gains.

Evaluation includes two clinical sources, several model families, three independent runs, classification and extraction tasks, and a training-size analysis. Appendix D.2 also compares synthetic pretraining with additional real-data pretraining under approximately matched training steps, strengthening the empirical case.

Two experienced annotators review the entire synthetic test split, adjudicate disagreements, correct rationales, and document errors. The generation prompt, 45 seed examples, filtering procedure, annotation guidelines, training configurations, and public release link support reuse. Together, the resource and downstream evidence warrant Findings publication.
weaknesses: The broad claim of consistent improvement needs qualification. Encoder-only NER gains are negligible, and the largest T5 improvement starts from a highly unstable baseline (25.44 ± 18.24 macro-F). Mamba and Llama models show little or no improvement on VA-SBDH. The evidence establishes benefits in particular model and data regimes more convincingly than general improvement across architectures and tasks.

The rare-category result is promising but uncertain: the headline housing-insecurity gain relies on only 18 positive test examples. Variation across three training seeds does not capture test-sample uncertainty. Class-reweighting or oversampling baselines would help establish the advantage over simpler remedies for imbalance. The real-data pretraining comparison is valuable, but its narrower category coverage does not isolate the effects of synthetic quality, coverage, and balance.

The distinctive rationale contribution has limited validation. DSS improves macro-F by only 0.66 points for T5 and 0.58 for FLAN-T5; the latter is not statistically significant (p = 0.36). Evaluation is confined to synthetic text, and extraction gains alone do not demonstrate transferred reasoning capability. Real-data evaluation of rationale-trained models would substantially strengthen this claim.

The proposed benchmark needs a more consistent annotation policy. Appendix E.2 accepts any compatible GPT-4 category for some ambiguous spans but requires the most specific category when adding annotations, potentially producing inconsistent reference labels for exact-match evaluation. The substantial corrections and additions are transparently reported, but aggregate agreement does not establish reliability separately for categories, presence, and temporality. Downstream experiments also do not directly evaluate temporal attribute prediction.

Reproducibility and reporting have remaining limitations. VA-SBDH is private, restricting independent replication of the clinical extraction and low-resource results. The manuscript does not clearly specify downstream prompt templates or all model-specific configurations. Dataset counts also need reconciliation: the stated training/development/test sizes sum to 8,727 rather than 8,767. These issues, together with the limited validation of the richer annotation features, constrain the main-conference case.
